tone_statements.quote: Syllable structure is CV(C), and each syllable is pronounced with a distinctive lexical tone. [...] Sangkong preserves the three Proto-Lolo-Burmese [PLB] tonal categories A, B, C intact in unchecked syllables. [...] In addition to these tones, a high rising tone is found in loan words and sandhi environments. [...] There are no generalized rules of tone sandhi operating across syllables in Sangkong, although certain lexical items do exhibit contextually determined tone changes

sources.citation: Handel, Zev. 2004. Review of Li Yongsui, A study of Sangkong [Sangkongyu yanjiu] (Beijing 2002, 403 pp.). Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 27(1): 111-142. DOI 10.32655/LTBA.27.1.05.
sources.note: Sec. 2 'Phonology' (pp. 113-119) summarises Li 2002 ch. 2: syllable is CV(C) 'and each syllable is pronounced with a distinctive lexical tone'; tones (p. 54 of Li) 55 A, 31 B (=DS), 33 C (=DL), 35 high rising in loans/sandhi/contractions; 'no generalized rules of tone sandhi'; phonetic alternations (fusion, nasal apocope, stop~nasal). The review nowhere mentions stress or accent; Li's 'strong/weak' syllables (pp. 121-122) are a semantic, not prosodic, notion.

tone.says: Sec. 2 'Phonology' (pp. 113-117) restates Li 2002 ch. 2: every CV(C) syllable bears a lexical tone; three inherited tones 55 (=PLB A), 31 (=B, with checked DS [42] as allotone), 33 (=C, with checked DL [44] as allotone), plus a fourth high-rising 35 confined to Mandarin/Tai loans, sandhi environments and contractions of low-high sequences; checked-syllable D category split by pitch (Li: earlier vowel length; Matisoff: initial class); no general tone-sandhi rules, only lexical tone changes ('thr…

sources.citation: Matisoff, James A. 1993. Sangkong 桑孔 of Yunnan: secondary 'verb pronominalization' in Southern Loloish. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 16(2): 123-142. DOI 10.32655/LTBA.16.2.07 (reprinted from Kitamura, Nishida & Nagano eds. 1994, Current Issues in Sino-Tibetan Linguistics, 588-607).
sources.note: Sec. 1.0 'Sangkong phonology' (pp. 123-124) lists initials, rhymes and four tones (55 high level, 33 mid level, 31 low falling, 35 high rising 'sandhi tone'); sec. 2.3 gives PLB tone correspondences. No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the 20 pages (a full-text search for stress/accent full scanned).

tone.quote: 2.3 Tones PLB *1 > SK 55 PLB *2 > SK 31 [...] Sangkong has the Loloish tonal split in stopped syllables (see Matisoff 1972), despite the relative well-preservedness of syllable-final consonants: more proof, if any were needed, that this split was conditioned by the syllable-initial consonant group.
tone.locator: sec. 2.3 'Tones', p. 126 (incl. footnote on constriction in the 35 tone); tone inventory sec. 1.3, p. 124
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.says: Sec. 1.3 'Tones' (p. 124) lists four tones: 55 high level, 33 mid level, 31 low falling, 35 high rising '(sandhi tone)'; sec. 2.3 (pp. 126-127) gives PLB > Sangkong tone reflexes (*1 > 55, *2 > 31, *3 > 33, *HS > 33 constricted, *LS > 31 constricted) and states that Sangkong has the Loloish tonal split in stopped syllables conditioned by the initial consonant group; words in the 35 tone sometimes constricted.
